newsitem.title: GERMANY: "Mr Financial Markets" to lead Deutsche forward.
newsitem.headline: "Mr Financial Markets" to lead Deutsche forward.

text.p: A tough PR job lies ahead for Rolf Breuer, the 58-year-old investment banker named on Wednesday as the man to steer Germany's powerful Deutsche Bank AG out of its mire of scandals of recent years.

Dubbed "Mr Financial Markets" for his role in stock market reforms here, Breuer is expected to forge a new openness when he takes over from Hilmar Kopper as chief executive at the notoriously reticent bank next year.

This eloquent and cosmopolitan investment banker, a relatively unknown quantity in terms of his banking philosophy, will be fighting hard to avoid the criticism and mistrust that dogged his predecessor.

Hilmar Kopper has never managed to shrug off the "peanuts" tag that attached to him in 1994, after he used the word to describe multi-million-mark losses caused by the collapse of the Schneider real estate empire, with which Deutsche was closely invloved.

Arguably, Breuer, also head of the German Stock Exchange's supervisory board and a tireless campaigner for an equity culture in Germany, will have somewhat better chances when he takes up the helm at Deutsche Bank on May 20 next year.

Much of Deutsche's past crises in its corporate lending business and property finance business have been put to rest, and Breuer's role in dealing with a scandal that erupted this year over funds mismanagement at the bank's MGAM unit in London was viewed as capable and decisive.

Four key heads have rolled at MGAM as a result of the incident and the bank is considering bringing the unit under stronger German control, a suggestion Breuer made almost immediately in an interview with the Financial Times newspaper.
Moreover, Breuer's devotion to Anglo-Saxon ideas such as shareholder value and corporate transparency should at least endear him to the international investment community.
"Breuer would certainly have made a slicker job of the 'peanuts' issue than Kopper was able to," said one banking analyst, who did not want to be identified.
"He has that kind of typical investment banker confidence, although I think the notion of being a Deutsche board member has gone to his head more than most," the analyst added.

Breuer, a board member at Deutsche since 1985, is now one of three top executives in charge of Deutsche's global investment banking business, one of the bank's biggest divisions and the main focus for its future ambitions.
"Because of his leadership in investment banking, Breuer really has risen to a very high level of responsibility in the past year," said Merck Finck banking analyst Konrad Becker.

"He hasn't had much of a profile so far but his appointment is certainly a sign that Deutsche is serious about investment banking," said Christine Winkler, analyst at Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechsel-Bank in Munich.
Breuer's banking career has followed traditional lines -- he began as a Deutsche Bank trainee in 1956, then took a law degree before returning to start a life-long career with the bank in 1966.
However the banker's stock exchange activities have been far more exceptional.
Breuer has spearheaded moves to harmonise the country's eight regional stock exchanges and to introduce electronic share trading -- both watersheds in Frankfurt's development as a financial centre.

Breuer believes that, once properly organised, Frankfurt is well equipped to compete with London and Paris as a key European financial centre and has dismissed the current emphasis on floor-based dealings as "a relic of old times."
